title: Primary science: sink or float
description: Four lessons from predicting sink-or-float to explaining steel ships: observe, manipulate a density micro-world, and transfer the idea.
assumptions: Densities are whole-number units; water is 10. No real experiments or network access are required.
stage1goal: Build the density comparison idea from evidence.
stage2goal: Explain and use the idea in new situations.
sink-or-float.title: Sink or float: predict first
sink-or-float.goal: Predict whether objects sink or float and check against evidence.
sink-or-float.reading: Whether something sinks depends on comparing its density with the liquid, not on its size or weight alone.
sink-or-float.worked.prompt: In your own words: what decides sink or float?
sink-or-float.worked.fb: Comparing object density with liquid density decides it.
sink-or-float.worked.hint: Look at the two numbers, not the size.
sink-or-float.worked.content: A wood block (density 6) floats in water (density 10); a stone (density 15) sinks.
sink-or-float.predict.prompt: A block of density 6 goes into water (10). What happens?
sink-or-float.predict.a.label: Floats: 6 < 10
sink-or-float.predict.b.label: Sinks: wood is heavy
sink-or-float.independent.prompt: An object suspends in water (10). What is its density?
sink-or-float.c1.a.label: Object density > liquid density
sink-or-float.c1.b.label: Object weight > liquid weight
sink-or-float.c1.b.fb: Weight alone is not the rule.
density-race.title: Density micro-world
density-race.goal: Manipulate object and liquid density and observe the submerged fraction.
density-race.reading: The submerged fraction equals object density divided by liquid density, capped at 1. Try pairs and watch the block.
density-race.worked.prompt: Why is exactly half of the block under the surface?
density-race.worked.fb: Because 5/10 = 0.5 of it must be submerged.
density-race.submerged.prompt: Object 8 in liquid 10: what percent is submerged?
density-race.submerged.hint: Turn the fraction into a percent.
density-race.independent.prompt: Raise the object to 12 while liquid stays 10. What happens?
density-race.independent.a.label: It floats higher
density-race.independent.a.fb: More dense means deeper, not higher.
density-race.independent.b.label: It sinks to the bottom
density-race.c1.b.fb: 0.7 is the part above, not below.
shape-and-ship.title: Why steel ships float
shape-and-ship.goal: Explain how shape changes average density so steel ships float.
shape-and-ship.reading: A steel ship encloses air, so its average density (steel + air + cargo) is less than water even though steel alone is denser.
shape-and-ship.struggle: A solid steel block sinks. Without numbers, explain how the same steel can float as a ship.
shape-and-ship.worked.prompt: What does the hull add that lowers average density?
shape-and-ship.worked.fb: Air-filled volume lowers the average density.
shape-and-ship.worked.hint: Think total mass divided by total volume.
shape-and-ship.worked.content: Steel density 78 > water 10, but a hull spreads that steel over a large air-filled volume.
shape-and-ship.independent.prompt: Which statement explains the floating ship?
shape-and-ship.independent.fb: Average density, not material density, decides.
shape-and-ship.independent.a.label: Average density of ship < water
shape-and-ship.independent.b.label: Steel becomes less dense in water
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.prompt: New situation: a submarine dives by taking water into its tanks. Why does that work?
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.fb: Flooding tanks raises average density above water.
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.a.labe: It adds air to the tanks
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.a.fb: Adding air would raise it, not dive.
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.b.labe: It floods tanks with water, raising average density
shape-and-ship.transfer-submarine.b.fb: More mass in same volume: average density rises above water.
shape-and-ship.c1.a.label: Steel is lighter than water
shape-and-ship.c1.b.label: Its average density is below water
explain-to-engineer.title: Explain it to an engineer
explain-to-engineer.goal: Teach the sink-or-float rule clearly enough that someone else can use it.
explain-to-engineer.reading: A good explanation states the comparison rule, gives one example, and names the exception-shaped case (suspension).
explain-to-engineer.worked.prompt: Say the rule in one sentence without numbers.
explain-to-engineer.worked.fb: Denser sinks, less dense floats, equal suspends.
explain-to-engineer.worked.content: Rule: compare densities. Example: 6 vs 10 floats. Special: equal suspends.
explain-to-engineer.teach-check.prompt: Explain to a friend why a tiny steel pin sinks but a huge steel ship floats.
explain-to-engineer.teach-check.fb: Pin: solid steel denser than water. Ship: air-filled hull lowers average density.
explain-to-engineer.teach-check.hint: Use average density for the ship.
explain-to-engineer.teach-check.content: A good explanation compares average density, not size.
explain-to-engineer.transfer-ice.prompt: New situation: ice floats in your drink. Which explanation uses the rule?
explain-to-engineer.transfer-ice.fb: Ice density ~9 < water 10: floats with ~90% submerged.
explain-to-engineer.transfer-ice.a.label: Ice is less dense than water, so it floats
explain-to-engineer.transfer-ice.b.label: Ice is colder, so it floats
explain-to-engineer.transfer-ice.b.fb: Temperature is not the rule here.
explain-to-engineer.c1.a.label: Sinking
explain-to-engineer.c1.b.label: Suspension
explain-to-engineer.c2.a.label: Object density / liquid density
explain-to-engineer.c2.b.label: Liquid density / object density
